heading: Background
html:
Ankle arthritis is usually post-traumatic (unlike hip/knee); hindfoot and midfoot arthritis are often degenerative or post-injury; hallux rigidus (first MTPJ arthritis) is the commonest arthritic condition of the foot. Surgical options — cheilectomy, fusion, joint replacement — are effective for the right patient, but conservative measures genuinely work and should be exhausted first.

Charcot foot masquerades as arthritis. A red, warm, swollen foot (± minimal pain) in a patient with diabetes or peripheral neuropathy is Charcot neuroarthropathy until excluded — same-day referral via the diabetes foot pathway, offload immediately. Do not wait for X-ray changes.

heading: Assessment
html:
• Localise the pain: first MTPJ (hallux rigidus), midfoot (arch collapse, dorsal exostoses), hindfoot/ankle (post-injury, stiffness on uneven ground).
  • Function: walking distance, work demands, footwear tolerance.
  • Examination: range of movement, deformity, tenderness, gait; check neurovascular status and skin.
  • Imaging: weight-bearing X-rays of the affected region — non-weight-bearing films underestimate deformity and joint loss.
  • Risk factors: diabetes (Charcot, healing risk), smoking (fusion non-union risk), inflammatory arthritis (consider rheumatology).

heading: Primary care management
html:
• Footwear — the highest-yield intervention: stiff-soled or rocker-bottom shoes reduce painful joint movement; wide/deep toe box for hallux rigidus.
  • Orthotics / insoles — via Single Access Point (030 3333 3001) triage to orthotist/podiatry.
  • Activity modification and weight management.
  • Analgesia: topical or oral NSAID (e.g. Naproxen) as per usual cautions.
  • Intra-articular corticosteroid injection (usually image-guided for foot/ankle joints) can give useful symptomatic relief and help localise the symptomatic joint.
  • Inflammatory features (multiple joints, prolonged morning stiffness, boggy swelling) → rheumatology, not orthopaedics.

heading: Who to refer
html:
Same day

  • Suspected Charcot foot — diabetes foot pathway, immediate offloading
  • Hot swollen joint with suspicion of infection — see hot swollen joint pathway

Routine orthopaedic referral — all of:

  • Arthritis confirmed on weight-bearing X-ray, correlating with the symptomatic site
  • Persistent significant pain or disability despite an adequate trial (typically ≥3–6 months) of footwear modification, orthotics and analgesia
  • Patient willing to consider surgical options (and accepts the trade-offs — e.g. fusion stiffness)

Include in referral: weight-bearing X-ray report, conservative measures tried and duration, diabetes/smoking status, functional impact, patient's view on surgery.

heading: Who not to refer
html:
• Patients who have not tried footwear modification and orthotics — SAP/MSK first; many avoid surgery altogether.
  • Radiographic arthritis with manageable symptoms.
  • Patients unwilling to consider surgery — continue conservative care.
  • Suspected inflammatory arthritis — rheumatology.
  • Flexible flat foot and forefoot problems without arthritis — existing foot & ankle pathways apply.
